10-01.text: Japan’s Coinage Law takes effect, moving the yen from silver to gold at 0.75 g of fine gold per yen.
10-01.source: Kahei Hō (Law No. 16 of 1897), Art. 20; National Archives of Japan

10-01.text: The U.S. Commission on International Exchange submits its report on a gold-exchange standard for China and other silver-using countries.
10-01.source: Report on the introduction of the gold-exchange standard into China and other silver-using countries, submitted to the Secretary of State October 1, 1903

10-03.text: At its Washington Annual Meeting, the IMF Board of Governors votes to allocate about SDR 9.5 billion in Special Drawing Rights over 1970-72.
10-03.source: IMF Board of Governors Resolution No. 24-12, 3 October 1969; de Vries, The International Monetary Fund 1966-1971, ch. 10; IMF, The SDR—Its Evolution and Prospects

10-04.text: Austria signs League Protocol No. III at Geneva, undertaking to surrender the right to issue paper money and to give a new bank of issue full autonomy.
10-04.source: League of Nations Treaty Series, vol. 12, No. 336, Protocol No. III, signed at Geneva, 4 October 1922

10-05.text: England’s Tower mint set new silver coins at about 92 parts silver in 100, so a shilling was silver again after years of copper-filled coins.
10-05.source: Henry Symonds, The English Coinages of Edward VI, British Numismatic Journal 11 (1915): commission sealed at Hampton Court on 5 October 1551, silver 11 oz 1 dwt fine, British Museum Additional MS 18759; C. E. Challis, Southwark Mint 1545–1551, British Numismatic Journal 33 (1964)

10-05.text: Italy’s Royal Decree-Law No. 1745 reduces the lira’s gold content from 0.07919 g to 0.04677 g of fine gold.
10-05.source: Banca d’Italia, Annual Report for 1936: Royal Decree-Law No. 1745 of 5 October 1936 reduced the gold content of the lira from 0.07919 to 0.04677 grammes fine; Gazzetta Ufficiale n. 231, 5 October 1936

10-06.text: Switzerland adopts the National Bank Act, requiring the Swiss National Bank to redeem its notes in gold or silver and to hold at least 40 percent metal cover.
10-06.source: Bundesgesetz über die Schweizerische Nationalbank vom 6. Oktober 1905, AS 22 47; Schweizerische Nationalbank, Geld- und währungspolitische Chronik; SNB, Die Schweizerische Nationalbank — Bilanz und Erfolgsrechnung (2007)

10-06.text: Congress gave the president power to regulate or stop exports of gold and silver coins and uncoined metal during the war.
10-06.source: Trading with the Enemy Act, ch. 106, 40 Stat. 411, approved 6 October 1917, §5(b), govinfo Statutes at Large; Guaranty Trust Company of New York, Trading with the Enemy: Act Approved October 6, 1917 (1917), digest of the export power over gold or silver coin or bullion

10-07.text: Public Law 96-389 requires the Treasury Secretary to establish and chair a commission on the role of gold in U.S. domestic and international monetary systems.
10-07.source: Public Law 96-389, sec. 10, 94 Stat. 1555, approved October 7, 1980; Anna J. Schwartz, Reflections on the Gold Commission Report, in Money in Historical Perspective (University of Chicago Press, 1987): established by an Act of Congress of October 7, 1980 (P.L. 96-389)

10-07.text: New York gold futures rose above $4,000 a troy ounce for the first time, a record price for gold.
10-07.source: Reuters, 7 October 2025, “US gold futures top $4,000 mark”: December futures settled at $4,004.40, the first close above $4,000 a troy ounce; Associated Press, 7 October 2025, gold futures above $4,000 a troy ounce for the first time

10-08.text: Massachusetts ordered full-weight Spanish silver dollars to pass at six local shillings, keeping the coins at home instead of shipping them out to be melted.
10-08.source: Records of the Governor and Company of the Massachusetts Bay, vol. IV, part II, session of 8 October 1672 (Shurtleff ed., pp. 533–534); Sylvester S. Crosby, The Early Coins of America (1875), p. 80

10-08.text: The Continental Congress voted to lift legal caps on gold and silver prices, so the metals could change hands at what people would actually pay.
10-08.source: Journals of the Continental Congress, vol. 12, 8 October 1778, pp. 990–992; Evans 16131, the Dunlap broadside “In Congress, October 8, 1778: Resolved, that all limitations of prices of gold and silver be taken off”

10-08.text: The War Production Board ordered U.S. gold mines it called unneeded for the war to close, to free scarce materials those mines used.
10-08.source: Federal Register, vol. 7, pp. 7992–7993 (9 October 1942): Limitation Order L-208, issued 8 October 1942; United States v. Central Eureka Mining Co., 357 U.S. 155 (1958)

10-09.text: Philadelphia banks stopped paying gold and silver coin for their notes, so holders could no longer turn that paper into metal on demand.
10-09.source: Warren E. Weber, Early State Banks in the United States, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis Quarterly Review, September 2006; John Joseph Wallis, The Depression of 1839 to 1843: States, Debts, and Banks, University of Maryland and NBER

10-09.text: The New York Fed made banks pay one percentage point more to borrow, as gold flowed out after Britain stopped paying gold for pounds.
10-09.source: Annual Report of the Federal Reserve Board for 1931: New York discount rate raised one point on October 9 as gold flowed out; Annual Report of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York for 1931: rate raised effective October 9 after Britain left gold and foreign demand for gold surged

10-10.text: The Philippines set aside a separate fund to keep its silver peso worth the same as a gold peso, so the silver coin would not slip below that gold value.
10-10.source: Philippine Commission Act No. 938, enacted 10 October 1903; Edwin W. Kemmerer, Gold and the Gold Standard (McGraw-Hill, 1944)

10-10.text: Vietnam ended the central bank’s sole right to make gold bars, letting licensed banks and companies produce them under the new rules.
10-10.source: Government of Vietnam, Decree No. 232/2025/ND-CP, in force 10 October 2025; Tuoi Tre Saigon Times, 10 October 2025, “SBV’s gold bar production monopoly ends today”

10-11.text: The Soviet State Bank was allowed to issue notes each equal to the old 10-ruble gold coin, giving trade a steady unit while the paper ruble kept falling.
10-11.source: Bank of Russia, Gold Tchervonets: a law dated 11 October 1922 let the State Bank issue a currency partially backed by gold; Decree of the Council of People’s Commissars of the RSFSR, 11 October 1922, Sobranie Uzakonenii 1922, no. 64, art. 827 (Electronic Library of Historical Documents): one note equalled 1 zolotnik 78.24 dolyas of pure gold, the old 10-ruble gold coin, with at least one quarter covered by precious metals and stable foreign currency, and exchange for gold left to a later act

10-11.text: After the paper mark collapsed, Germany’s coinage law took effect and set one Reichsmark equal to 1/2790 of a kilogram of pure gold.
10-11.source: Deutsche Bundesbank, purchasing-power comparisons: the Reichsmark was introduced on 11 October 1924 and equalled one Goldmark, defined as 1/2790 kg of fine gold; Münzgesetz of 30 August 1924 (RGBl. II p. 254), put into force on 11 October 1924 by the Zweite Verordnung of 10 October 1924 (RGBl. II p. 383)

10-12.text: Brazil ordered its Minas Gerais gold fields to exchange panned gold dust for coin or small notes, and to stamp Spanish silver coins before they passed.
10-12.source: Alvará de 12 de outubro de 1808, Coleção das Leis do Brasil de 1808, p. 145: panned gold dust exchanged for coin or printed notes, and Spanish silver pesos to pass only with the royal stamp; Ângelo Alves Carrara, Mineração, produção rural e espaços urbanos em Minas Gerais: 1808-1835 (2006): the alvará of 12 October regulated printed notes for exchanging gold dust

10-12.text: Finland's central bank stopped paying gold for its notes for the time being, so the markka could no longer be cashed in gold on demand.
10-12.source: Bank of England Archives, OV48/9, report of 21 January 1932: Finland suspended the gold standard on 12 October 1931; Jaakko Autio, Lama ja raha, Bank of Finland (1992): on 12 October 1931 the bank stopped redeeming its notes in gold

10-13.text: Castile ordered fine weights so missing gold in a light gold coin could be measured, and a short coin would not pass as a full one.
10-13.source: Pragmática of Valladolid, 13 October 1488, quoted by Pablo Rueda Rodríguez-Vila, OMNI no. 12 (2018); Josefina Mateu Ibars, Estudios en memoria del Profesor D. Salvador de Moxó, vol. II (Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 1982)

10-13.text: Costa Rica set up a government mint in San José to strike its own gold and silver coins, so people would not have to rely on scarce foreign money.
10-13.source: Gilbert Laporte Soto, Tipos de cambio extranjeros durante la vigencia del sistema bimetalista (1821–1872); José A. Vargas Zamora and Manuel B. Chacón Hidalgo, Revista Herencia 35, no. 1 (2022), Universidad de Costa Rica

10-13.text: Spain ordered paper certificates to stand in for its silver coins, while the bank kept an equal amount of silver coin until new coins could be struck.
10-13.source: Gaceta de Madrid, no. 289 (15 October 1936), decree given in Madrid on 13 October 1936; Miguel Martorell Linares, Una guerra, dos pesetas (UNED)

10-14.text: Westminster tested sample gold and silver coins from the English mint at Calais, to show the coins were full weight and not short of metal.
10-14.source: Calendar of Patent Rolls 1422–1429, pp. 337–340, recording a trial on 14 October 1424; Martin Allen, The output and profits of the Calais mint, 1349–1450, British Numismatic Journal 80 (2010), citing that roll and TNA C 66/419

10-14.text: Chile set the peso at one-third of its old official gold weight, in line with the market, so a gold standard could work again.
10-14.source: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, Decreto Ley 606, dated and promulgated 14 October 1925: one peso equals 0.183057 grams of fine gold; Camilo Carrasco, Banco Central de Chile: that monetary law cut the peso’s gold content from 18 pence to 6, and the bank’s coin record dates Decreto Ley 606 to 14 October 1925

10-14.text: Spot silver hit a record high because London ran short of bars, the form in which that market delivers the metal.
10-14.source: Reuters, 14 October 2025: spot silver hit a record high of $53.60 an ounce; The Hindu BusinessLine, updated 14 October 2025: silver rose to a record high that Tuesday as supply was short

10-15.text: The U.S. Mint handed over 1,758 silver dollars, the first the country had made. The press could not strike a coin that wide, so the design came out weak.
10-15.source: John Adams proclamation, 22 July 1797, Founders Online: silver coinage at the U.S. Mint commenced on 15 October 1794; National Museum of American History: 1,758 silver dollars, the first minted for circulation, were coined on 15 October 1794 and delivered to the Mint Director

10-15.text: Germany set up a bank whose notes used a unit equal to a weight of pure gold, with charges on land and industry behind them, after the paper mark collapsed.
10-15.source: Verordnung über die Errichtung der Deutschen Rentenbank, 15 October 1923, Reichsgesetzblatt I 1923, pp. 963–966: a Goldmark is 1/2790 kg of fine gold, and the bank’s notes rest on charges on land and industry; United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: the German government established the Rentenbank on 15 October 1923

10-16.text: The Continental Congress ordered a mint for gold, silver, and copper, and set the dollar value of each, so foreign coins could become one national money.
10-16.source: Ordinance for Establishing a Mint, done by the United States in Congress Assembled on 16 October 1786, Journals of the Continental Congress, vol. 31, pp. 876–878, and the printed ordinance Evans 20074 (Library of Congress); U.S. Mint, Timeline of the United States Mint

10-16.text: Britain ordered several colonies to take its coins as money, but no one had to accept silver above forty shillings, so a large payment had to be made in gold.
10-16.source: Robert Chalmers, A History of Currency in the British Colonies (H.M. Stationery Office, 1893), Order in Council and Proclamation of 16 October 1852; B. W. Fernando, Ceylon Currency: British Period (Ceylon Government Press, 1939), reprinting that order

10-17.text: France's national assembly threw out a local order that would have forced people to give up coins and metal bars for paper notes that were losing trust.
10-17.source: Archives parlementaires, vol. 76, session of 17 October 1793: the Convention quashed the Haute-Garonne order to exchange coined money or bullion for paper notes; University of Chicago Revolutionary Laws corpus, decree of 26 vendémiaire Year II (17 October 1793) cancelling that order

10-17.text: Spain ordered district towns to appoint a sworn tester of gold and silver, so a fake gold coin, gold leaf over copper, could be caught and kept out of use.
10-17.source: Ministry of Hacienda circular, copy authenticated at Madrid on 17 October 1825 by Luis López Ballesteros (Biblioteca Digital de Castilla y León): district towns must appoint assayers of gold and silver after a fake eight-escudo gold coin with the leaf soldered over copper; Antonio García González, Tratado teórico-práctico para conocimiento de las monedas falsas españolas (1882), royal order of 17 October 1825

10-18.text: Britain ordered the Sydney mint to strike gold coins of the same weight and purity as the sovereign, its main gold coin, so Australian gold could become coin.
10-18.source: New Zealand Government Gazette, No. 13, 26 June 1855, printing the Orders in Council made at Windsor on 18 October 1854; Canada Gazette proclamation given at Windsor on 14 May 1868, reciting that order: gold coins struck at the Sydney mint were to match the British sovereign in weight and fineness

10-18.text: Uruguay let the government strike up to three million pesos in silver coins, nine-tenths pure, so more of its own silver money could circulate.
10-18.source: Ley No. 2208, Compilación de Leyes y Decretos, 1892, promulgated at Montevideo on 18 October 1892; Banco de la República Oriental del Uruguay, Memoria y Balance 1918: that law authorized coining up to three million pesos in silver of the same standard as the 1877 coins, nine-tenths fine

10-19.text: Spain made the peseta its money unit and ordered gold and silver coins to match France, Belgium, Italy, and Switzerland in weight and purity.
10-19.source: Decreto of the Provisional Government, signed at Madrid on 19 October 1868 by Laureano Figuerola, reprinted in Centro de Estudios Políticos y Constitucionales, Las leyes monetarias de 1868 y 1946: the peseta is the money unit and gold and silver coins are ordered (Gaceta de Madrid, 20 October 1868); Banco de España, History of peseta coins and notes: the peseta was established by a government decree enacted on 19 October 1868

10-19.text: Congress approved a law repealing the rule that set the dollar's official gold value, with that repeal waiting until new world money rules took effect.
10-19.source: Public Law 94-564, 90 Stat. 2660, approved October 19, 1976: section 6 repeals the statute that set the dollar's legal gold value, and section 9 delays that repeal until the amended IMF articles take effect; B. Dianne Pauls, Federal Reserve Bulletin, November 1990: that amendment was approved on October 19, 1976, and Congress repealed the Par Value Modification Act

10-20.text: Britain declared a new silver coin, the half-crown, lawful money at two shillings and sixpence, so it could pass in everyday payments.
10-20.source: London Gazette, 21 October 1820, issue 17644: proclamation given at Carlton-House on 20 October 1820 making the new silver half-crown current and lawful money at two shillings and sixpence; The E-Sylum, vol. 25, no. 42, Numismatic Bibliomania Society: George IV issued that proclamation on 20 October 1820

10-20.text: London gold jumped from near the official $35 an ounce to about $40, a sign the dollar's gold link was under strain.
10-20.source: FRUS 1958-1960, vol. IV, doc. 56, memorandum of 25 October 1960: London gold peaked at about $40.60 an ounce on 20 October; Robert L. Hetzel, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Economic Quarterly, Spring 1996: on 20 October 1960 the London price shot from close to $35 to $40 an ounce

10-20.text: The U.S. Mint put American Eagle gold coins on sale, its first gold bullion coins, bringing a new United States gold coin to market.
10-20.source: Annual Report of the Director of the Mint for the fiscal year ended 30 September 1986: sales of the Gold American Eagle coins were scheduled to begin on 20 October 1986; Los Angeles Times, 20 October 1986, Associated Press: the American Eagle, a new U.S. gold coin, went on sale that day

10-21.text: Spain put old small coins that still held a little silver back into use at their old value, and the king kept half of what people turned in.
10-21.source: Josefina Mateu Ibars, Estudios en memoria del Profesor D. Salvador de Moxó, vol. II (Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 1982): pragmatic given at El Escorial on 21 October 1654 that old calderilla be stamped again and pass at its former value, with owners receiving half and the crown the other half; Ángel Gómez Paz, La moneda de vellón castellana en el reinado de Felipe IV, Ab Initio, extraordinary no. 1 (2011): on 21 October 1654 that calderilla, the old coin minted before 1599 with a little silver, was allowed to circulate again

10-21.text: Spain said an old debt payable in gold coins had to be paid in those coins at the higher value already set for them, as with silver.
10-21.source: Josefina Mateu Ibars, Estudios en memoria del Profesor D. Salvador de Moxó, vol. II (Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 1982): council order at Madrid, 21 October 1686, that debts payable in gold escudos or doubloons be paid in those coins at the higher value set on 14 October, as with debts payable in silver; Cecilia Font de Villanueva, Monetary reform in times of Charles II, Universidad Carlos III de Madrid Working Paper 06-07 (2006): the consultation published on 21 October applied to outstanding gold debts the same measures already set for silver

10-22.text: Buenos Aires let its provincial bank issue notes in the peso defined in gold, rather than in the ordinary paper peso.
10-22.source: Registro Oficial de la Provincia de Buenos Aires, 1870, Law 628, and the contract approved by President Sarmiento on 9 November 1869: both cite the Law of 22 October 1866 for the bank’s metallic notes in pesos fuertes; Ricardo Panza, Reseña monetaria y del tipo de cambio argentinos: that provincial law authorized metallic notes of 20 pesos fuertes

10-22.text: Roosevelt announced a government market for newly mined U.S. gold, with the price set in Washington, so officials could steer the dollar's gold value.
10-22.source: American Presidency Project, Franklin D. Roosevelt Fireside Chat, 22 October 1933; Commercial and Financial Chronicle, 3 February 1934 (FRASER): the Sunday night address of 22 October 1933 announced a government market for newly mined gold so the United States could control the gold value of the dollar

10-24.text: France ordered each new gold or silver coin to count for fewer livres in two later steps, so each livre would mean more metal and food would cost less.
10-24.source: Arrêt du Conseil d'État du 24 octobre 1720, transcribed from the Superior Council of New France register: new gold and silver coins stay at the September rates until 1 December, then the silver écu falls from 9 livres to 7 livres 10 sols and is set to fall to 6 livres on 1 January; François R. Velde, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Chronicle of a Deflation Unforetold (revised 2007): the decree of 24 October 1720 resumed that cut for the benefit of trade and to reduce the price of foodstuffs

10-24.text: Costa Rica made gold, not silver, the base of its money, and set the colón as 778 milligrams of gold nine-tenths pure, because silver's value kept swinging.
10-24.source: Sistema Costarricense de Información Jurídica, Ley N.º 3, Decreto de 24 de octubre de 1896, preamble and Art. II: gold replaces silver as the base, and the colón is 778 milligrams of gold of 900 thousandths fine, dated at Cartago on 24 October 1896; José A. Vargas Zamora, Revista Reflexiones 86-1 (2007), Universidad de Costa Rica: the decree of 24 October 1896 set the colón at 778 milligrams of gold nine-tenths fine
